title: PS5 & Xbox TV Calibration: HGiG vs DTM, ALLM & HDMI 2.1 Setup Guide
description: Comprehensive television calibration guide for PS5 and Xbox Series X: HGiG clipping calibration, Dynamic Tone Mapping pitfalls, ALLM activation, 120Hz bandwidth, and 48 Gbps cables.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: For optimal gaming HDR on PS5 and Xbox Series X, set your television tone mapping to HGiG before running the console HDR calibration wizard. Unlike Dynamic Tone Mapping (DTM) which dynamically alters luminance frame-by-frame and causes highlight blowouts, HGiG disables TV tone processing and lets the console clip precisely at the television physical peak luminance (e.g. ~800 nits on standard WOLED, ~1500 nits on QD-OLED). Enable Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM) and verify Ultra High Speed 48 Gbps HDMI 2.1 cabling for 4K 120Hz 10-bit RGB.
articleHtml:
Mastering Console HDR: The Engineering Principles of Television Calibration

Connecting a modern PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X to a 4K television is plug-and-play, but achieving pristine visual fidelity, accurate specular highlights, and minimum input latency requires understanding how game engines, console video output pipelines, and television display processors negotiate High Dynamic Range (HDR) metadata.

Critical TV Picture Mode Comparison

HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group)

Recommended for Gaming. Television disables internal tone mapping above hard clip point. Game engine masters highlights directly to your panel's true nit capability without double processing.

Dynamic Tone Mapping (DTM)

Not Recommended for Grading. Television alters scene luminance dynamically per frame. Produces artificially bright shadows and blows out specular cloud/sun details.

Game Optimizer / Game Mode

Mandatory for Input Latency. Bypasses post-processing frame buffers, dropping input lag from 80+ ms down to 4 to 12 ms with full ALLM support.

1. HGiG vs Dynamic Tone Mapping: Preventing the Double-Tonemap Trap

The most common calibration mistake made by console owners is leaving television Dynamic Tone Mapping (DTM) enabled while calibrating HDR in the console system settings.

To comprehend why this degrades visual fidelity, consider how tone mapping functions:

  • Television Hard Clipping vs Soft Roll-Off: Every television panel possesses a physical maximum luminance ceiling (e.g. 750 nits on traditional LG WOLED panels, 1,400 nits on Samsung QD-OLEDs, or 2,500+ nits on premium Mini-LED displays). If a game outputs a specular highlight of 2,000 nits to an 800-nit television, the television must compress or clip those values.
  • The HGiG Protocol: Established by Sony, Microsoft, and major display manufacturers, HGiG instructs the television to disable internal tone curve processing and report its exact clipping point to the console. During system HDR calibration, the console renders calibration symbols until the white patch matches the television's physical limit. From that point on, the game engine maps highlights with a 1:1 hard clip, preserving creator intent and fine texture details in direct sunlight, fires, and explosions.
  • The Double-Tonemapping Trap: When DTM is turned on, the television analyzes incoming frames in real time and artificially boosts darker scenes while compressing bright highlights to make the overall image "pop". If you calibrate the console HDR wizard with DTM active, the television dynamically shifts the calibration screen while you are adjusting the sliders! The console records erroneous peak luminance metadata, resulting in double-tonemapped, washed-out images with blown-out highlights during actual gameplay.

2. Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM) and Input Lag Optimization

Modern televisions employ sophisticated image processing suites—including motion interpolation (MEMC), digital noise reduction (DNR), edge sharpening, and dynamic contrast. While advantageous for low-bitrate cable broadcasts, these algorithms buffer multiple uncompressed frames in video memory, adding 50 to 90 milliseconds of processing latency.

HDMI 2.1 introduced Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM). When ALLM is enabled on your console and television, the console transmits a specialized Consumer Electronics Control (CEC) flag over the HDMI link as soon as a game application launches. The television automatically switches from its standard picture mode to its specialized low-latency Game Mode, completely disabling processing frame buffers.

In certified Game Mode on modern OLED and fast LCD televisions, input latency plummets from 80 ms down to:

  • 60Hz Signal: 9.0 ms to 13.5 ms.
  • 120Hz Signal: 4.5 ms to 6.2 ms (approaching dedicated esports PC monitor speeds).

3. HDMI 2.1 Video Bandwidth & 48 Gbps Cable Certification

Ninth-generation consoles deliver uncompressed 4K video at 120Hz with 10-bit HDR and 4:4:4 uncompressed chroma subsampling. Transmitting this massive data stream requires significant physical bandwidth across the HDMI cable:

$$\text{4K 120Hz 10-bit 4:4:4 Bandwidth} \approx 40.1\text{ Gbps (FRL 5 / FRL 6)}$$

Older HDMI 2.0 cables (labeled 'High Speed' or 'Premium High Speed') are electrically limited to 18.0 Gbps using Transition-Minimized Differential Signaling (TMDS). If an 18 Gbps cable is connected to a 120Hz console signal, the system must either downsample color to 4:2:0 chroma (causing color fringing around text and crosshairs) or drop refresh rate to 60Hz.

To guarantee full fidelity, ensure you utilize an Ultra High Speed HDMI certified cable capable of 48 Gbps Fixed Rate Link (FRL). The cable included in the retail box of both the PS5 and Xbox Series X is fully 48 Gbps certified.

4. Step-by-Step Calibration Sequence for PS5 and Xbox

  1. Enable Ultra HD Deep Color on TV: In your television settings, navigate to General > External Devices > HDMI Settings and set the console's HDMI port to 'HDMI Ultra HD Deep Color' (LG) or 'Enhanced Format (VRR)' (Sony).
  2. Activate Game Mode & Set Tone Mapping to HGiG: Switch television picture mode to 'Game Optimizer' or 'Game'. Enter Advanced Picture Settings > Brightness > Tone Mapping and select HGiG (or 'Off' if HGiG is unavailable). Set TV Sharpness to neutral (0 on LG/Samsung, 50 on Sony) to avoid artificial edge halos.
  3. Run PlayStation 5 HDR Calibration: On PS5, navigate to Settings > Screen and Video > Adjust HDR:
    • Screen 1 (Max Peak Luminance): Press D-Pad Up until the sun symbol disappears completely, then stop on the exact click where it vanishes. (On an 800-nit OLED, this corresponds to approximately 14 to 16 clicks).
    • Screen 2 (Max Full-Frame Luminance): Repeat identically until the symbol just vanishes.
    • Screen 3 (Black Level / Min Luminance): Press D-Pad Down all the way to 0 clicks (bottom limit) to guarantee true absolute black (0.000 nits) on OLED displays.
  4. Run Xbox Series X HDR Calibration: Navigate to Settings > General > TV & display options > Calibrate HDR. Follow the test screens to align maximum clipping and black levels with your panel's hardware ceiling.

faq.q: Why does my image look darker when switching from DTM to HGiG?
faq.a: Dynamic Tone Mapping artificially raises average picture level (APL), making midtones and shadows much brighter than mastered. HGiG restores creator intent: shadowed interiors appear realistically dim, while sunlight and explosions accurately punch out at maximum panel brightness.

faq.q: What should I set Sharpness to in Game Mode?
faq.a: Sharpness should be set to neutral (0 on LG and Samsung, 50 on Sony). Increasing sharpness adds artificial high-contrast white halos around fine geometry, creating visual ringing and aliasing.

faq.q: What is the difference between RGB Full and RGB Limited?
faq.a: RGB Full maps color channels from 0 to 255 (standard for PC monitors), while RGB Limited maps from 16 to 235 (traditional television broadcast standard). Both the console and TV should be left on 'Auto' so they negotiate matching levels; mismatched ranges cause crushed shadows or washed-out grays.

faq.q: How can I test whether my TV is properly calibrated?
faq.a: Use our TV & Gaming Display Capability Checker and HDR Display Calibration Patterns tools to verify refresh rates, 10-bit banding gradients, and 4:4:4 chroma text clarity.
